nameStory: This lovely butterfly gets its name from the distinctive metallic silver spots that border its hindwings, creating a shimmering band that catches the light as it flutters by. The word 'fritillary' comes from the Latin 'fritillus,' meaning dice box, referring to the checkered pattern on many species in this group.
description: The American Silver-bordered Fritillary is a medium-sized orange butterfly adorned with black spots and lines across its wings. Its most striking feature is the row of bright silver spots along the edges of its hindwings, which gleam like tiny mirrors in sunlight. These butterflies have a wingspan of about 1.5 to 2 inches and belong to the brush-footed butterfly family, meaning their front legs are reduced and brush-like rather than used for walking.

idTips.label: Silver hindwing border
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive row of metallic silver spots along the outer edge of the hindwings that shimmer and catch light as the butterfly moves

idTips.label: Orange base color
idTips.description: Wings are bright orange-red with a warm, almost burnt-orange hue that's more vibrant than faded autumn leaves

idTips.label: Black spotting pattern
idTips.description: Dark black spots and lines create a complex checkered pattern across the upper wing surfaces, with spots varying in size from tiny dots to larger crescents

idTips.label: Wing size and flight
idTips.description: Medium-sized with a somewhat erratic, bouncing flight pattern close to the ground, often landing with wings spread horizontally

idTips.label: Hindwing underside
idTips.description: The underside of hindwings shows a mix of orange, cream, and brown patches with those telltale silver spots standing out like polished metal

habitat: American Silver-bordered Fritillaries prefer open, sunny areas like meadows, fields, bogs, and woodland clearings throughout New England. They're especially fond of damp or wet areas where their host plants, various violet species, thrive in the understory. You'll often spot them nectaring on flowers in sunny openings within or adjacent to forested areas.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, typically appearing in May when violets are blooming and temperatures warm consistently.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight time runs through June and July when adults are most active, mating, and laying eggs on violet leaves in sunny spots.
seasonality.fall: Flight period may extend into early August in some areas, but adults become increasingly scarce as they complete their breeding cycle.
seasonality.winter: Overwinters as caterpillars, hidden among leaf litter and low vegetation, completely inactive until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Scientists recently discovered through DNA analysis that what we thought was one widespread fritillary species was actually two distinct species all along - the American Silver-bordered Fritillary and the Small Pearl-bordered Fritillary were living secret double lives until genomic sequencing revealed their true identities!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Meadow Fritillary, but the Meadow Fritillary lacks those distinctive silver spots on the hindwings and instead has yellowish or pale spots. Remember: silver spots = Silver-bordered, no silver = Meadow Fritillary.
contextualKnowledge: This species was previously lumped together with the Small Pearl-bordered Fritillary (Boloria selene) under a single species name until recent genetic studies revealed they were distinct species. In North America, there's also a subspecies called the Dark-bordered Fritillary that has darker wing borders.
compareHints: Among its Boloria relatives in New England, the American Silver-bordered Fritillary is distinguished by its prominent silver hindwing spots, while the Meadow Fritillary lacks silver markings entirely. The Bog Fritillary is much more restricted to specific bog habitats and has a different pattern of pale spots rather than true silver ones.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Boloria relatives in New England, the meadow fritillary is the most widespread and the one you're most likely to encounter in typical meadow habitats.
Compared to other Boloria fritillaries in New England, the Arctic fritillary is the most cold-adapted and northern in distribution.
